items.prose: Four lines from a trading desk's chat.
items.question: Which one is a statement?

options.text: The spread on this bond is 12 basis points
Is the spread wide today?
options.why: You picked a question. It asks rather than claims.

options.text: The spread is wide
options.why: You kept “wide”. Without a threshold it cannot be marked true or false.

options.text: Tighten the spread before the close
options.why: You picked an instruction. It is not true or false.

feedback.correct: Right. It names a number that can be checked.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line that can be marked true or false.

explain.text: Only the line giving the spread as 12 basis points makes a definite claim. A quote screen can mark it true or false.

items.prose: Fill one row of a truth table: the row where $P$ is false and $Q$ is true.
items.question: Fill in each value with T or F.

feedback.correct: F, T, T. **And** fails, **or** holds, and $\lnot P$ is true.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. **And** needs both, **or** needs one, and **not** flips.

byKey.r0c2: **And** needs both parts true, and $P$ is false.
byKey.r0c3: **Or** needs one true part, and $Q$ is true.
byKey.r0c4: $P$ is F, so $\lnot P$ is T.

explain.text: With $P$ false, $P \land Q$ is F. With $Q$ true, $P \lor Q$ is T. $\lnot P$ flips F to T.

items.prose: Rule: **if an order is a market order, it was sent before 4pm**. Each card is one order: its type on one side and its send time on the other.
items.question: Which cards must you turn over to check the rule? Tap each one.

feedback.correct: The Market card and the 4:20pm card.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn only the cards that could hide a breach.

byKey.confirm: You turned the 3:15pm card. An order sent before 4pm keeps the rule whatever its type. The 4:20pm card could be a market order.
byKey.lim: The rule makes no demand on limit orders.
byKey.t315: An order sent at 3:15pm keeps the rule whatever its type.

explain.text: A breach is a market order sent at 4pm or later. Only the Market card and the 4:20pm card could show one.

items.prose: Rule: **if a bond is investment grade, its rating is BBB− or above**. A second sentence reads: **if a bond's rating is below BBB−, it is not investment grade**.
items.question: What is the second sentence, relative to the rule?

options.text: Its contrapositive, so it says the same thing
Its converse, so it may differ
options.why: The converse would start from the rating: if rated BBB− or above, then investment grade.

options.text: Its inverse, so it may differ
options.why: The inverse would start “if a bond is not investment grade”.

options.text: Its negation, so it contradicts the rule
options.why: A negation is a breach: an investment grade bond rated below BBB−.

feedback.correct: Right. It negates both parts and swaps them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the rule as $P \Rightarrow Q$ and compare.

explain.text: With $P$ “investment grade” and $Q$ “BBB− or above”, the second sentence is $\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P$. That is the contrapositive, which agrees with the rule on every row.

items.prose: Weekly returns of three stocks over four weeks.
items.question: Which claims are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: There is a week in which every stock rose
Every stock rose in some week
In every week, some stock rose
options.why: Week 2 breaks it: all three stocks fell.

options.text: Some stock rose in every week
options.why: Each row has a fall: S1 in W2, S2 in W1, S3 in W2.

feedback.correct: Right. Week 3 is a shared witness, so the weaker claim follows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each claim, decide what a witness must look like.

explain.text: In week 3 all three stocks rose, so $\exists w\ \forall s$ holds. That shared week is also every stock's witness. Week 2 has no rise, and every row has a fall.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the integer that 3 multiplies to give 12.

byKey.thirtysix: You multiplied 12 by 3. The witness is $12 \div 3$.

explain.text: $3x = 12$ gives $x = 4$, an integer. So 4 is a witness and the claim is true.

items.prose: A report says: **it is not the case that the fund beat its benchmark and stayed within its risk limit**.
items.question: Which sentence says the same?

options.text: The fund did not beat its benchmark, or it did not stay within its risk limit
The fund did not beat its benchmark, and it did not stay within its risk limit
options.why: You negated both parts but kept **and**. De Morgan switches it to **or**.

options.text: The fund lagged its benchmark, or it broke its risk limit
options.why: You turned “did not beat” into “lagged”. Matching the benchmark does not beat it either.

options.text: The fund did not beat its benchmark
options.why: You negated one part only. Breaking the risk limit also makes the report true.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate each part and switch the connective.

explain.text: De Morgan's law turns $\lnot(P \land Q)$ into $\lnot P \lor \lnot Q$. “Did not beat” keeps the tie, so it is not the same as “lagged”.

items.prose: Rule: **if an order is over £1m, it needs a second approval**.
items.question: Which sentence describes a breach of the rule?

options.text: An order over £1m went through without a second approval
If an order is over £1m, it does not need a second approval
options.why: You wrote a new rule. A breach is one order: large and unapproved.

options.text: An order under £1m had a second approval
options.why: Extra approval on a small order breaks nothing.

options.text: If an order is under £1m, it does not need a second approval
options.why: That is the inverse, which the rule never mentioned.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the one case the rule forbids.

explain.text: The rule is false only for an order over £1m with no second approval. That case is its negation.

items.prose: Claim: **for every day this month, there is a desk with positive P&L**.
items.question: Which sentence is its negation?

options.text: There is a day this month on which every desk had P&L of zero or less
There is a day on which some desk had P&L of zero or less
options.why: You flipped only the first quantifier. “There is a desk” must become “every desk”.

options.text: There is a day on which every desk lost money
options.why: You turned “not positive” into “lost”. A desk at exactly zero is not positive either.

options.text: On every day, every desk had P&L of zero or less
options.why: You kept “every day”. One bad day is enough to deny the claim.

feedback.correct: Right. $\lnot \forall d\ \exists k$ is $\exists d\ \forall k\ \lnot$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Flip each quantifier in order, then negate the inside exactly.

explain.text: The claim is $\forall d\ \exists k$, positive. Its negation is $\exists d\ \forall k$, not positive: zero or less. Breaking even counts, so “lost money” is too strong.
